opening.headline: As conversations grow longer, one understands why models lose track of earlier content and incur higher costs, and learns the principle of designing which elements to include and which to exclude from the context.
body: At the beginning of the task, agents follow instructions well; however, after dozens of turns, they begin to forget the previously established rules. During this time, the entire history of past conversations is re-input every turn, continuously increasing cost. Even if the context window grows larger, this problem does not disappear.

In this lesson, we first examine what fills the context window and why recall degrades as token count increases. Then, we explore the difference between prompt engineering and context engineering, learn the goal of identifying the smallest set of high-signal tokens, and understand how to dynamically retrieve necessary information on an as-needed basis through JIT (Just-In-Time) context.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the purpose of context engineering
You can distinguish between what to put in the context and what to leave out.

screens.title: The longer the conversation goes on, the more you miss and pay.
screens.lead: Move the slider to see how the context and behavior differ depending on the number of turns the same agent continues working. The number of turns is provided as an example for illustrative purposes.

visual.alt: As turn increases, input tokens continue to rise, and the recall of prior content gradually fades, depicted by two curves.
labels: The extent of accurately recalling the previous content

data.controlLabel: Turn number to continue the operation

stops.body: The context includes the system prompt and a few previous conversations, along with some tool results. The model follows the initial instructions well. Each turn reinputs the entire prior conversation, but the volume is small and incurs minimal cost.

Tool results and responses accumulate, making the input visibly larger. Since all previous content is re-entered before each turn, both cost and delay increase. Initial instructions and previously established rules begin to get squeezed among the large amounts of content.

As input grows larger, models become more prone to missing earlier content. This phenomenon, where the ability to accurately recall information from context deteriorates as the number of tokens increases, is known as context rot. Simply increasing the size of the context window does not automatically result in better performance.

screens.outro: Therefore, designing what to include and what to exclude becomes necessary. First, let us reflect on your own experience.

screens.title: Think about the point where quality deteriorates.
screens.lead: After first thinking through the question mentally and making a choice, the instructor's thought process is revealed. Answers are not entered or submitted.

items.prompt: Have you ever noticed the point at which quality starts to degrade during prolonged operations?
items.answer: This is typically when the process takes longer and tool wear begins to accumulate. Instead of suddenly failing at a specific turn number, it manifests gradually as a slow decline in precision. Therefore, it is difficult to detect this point in advance.

items.prompt: At that time, what did the agent miss? The initial instruction, the previously defined rules—think about the file location.
items.answer: The instructions and rules that were primarily located at the beginning, along with the previously verified facts, become blurred. This can be viewed as a result of the model's attention becoming sparse across a large number of tokens, rather than the model having forgotten them.

items.prompt: At that point, what was most accumulated in the context?
items.answer: The largest share consists of typical tool outputs—such as search result bodies, full file contents, logs, and similar items. Knowing what occupies the majority is the first step in designing context.

screens.outro: Let us examine the composition of the context window to understand why this phenomenon occurs.

screens.title: Context window and attention budget
screens.lead: When you hover over or select the terms underlined in the text, a brief description appears. Review the context window to see what it contains and understand why limited resources are used.

visual.alt: Showing the context pane as a single column, with the system prompt, tool definitions, conversation history, tool results, and output divided across the diagram.
labels: The more tokens there are, the thinner the attention budget becomes.

data.text: context window consists of all text that the model can reference when generating a response, corresponding to the model's working memory. According to the Claude documentation, system prompts, all content within messages (including tool results, images, and documents), and tool definitions are all included in the context window, as are the model's generated outputs and extended reasoning. While a larger context window enables handling of more complex requests, having more context does not automatically lead to better performance. As the number of tokens increases, accuracy and recall degrade due to context rot. Anthropic describes this phenomenon as Warning budget. In transformer models, every token observes all other tokens, so with n tokens, there are n² relationships formed, and as the length increases, attention becomes increasingly sparse. However, performance degrades gradually rather than sharply, and the degree of gradual decline varies by model.

terms.tip: This is the range of all text that the model can reference when generating a response. It includes the output, and the size varies depending on the model.
The phenomenon where the ability to accurately recall information within a context decreases as the number of tokens in the context increases.
This is a finite attention resource used when the model reads a large context. A portion of it is consumed every time a new token is added.
When there are n tokens, the number of pairs where each token looks at another doubles to n squared.

screens.outro: If the budget is limited, one must decide what to include. This process is called context engineering.

screens.title: Context Engineering and Signal-to-Noise Ratio
screens.lead: Alternate between the two states and compare how the same operation's context differs when it is noisy versus curated.

visual.alt: A diagram comparing a noisy context and a curated context for the same task.
labels: A set of instructions listing all rules

states.label: Noisy context
states.body: The system prompt lists all possible rules in every scenario, with multiple tools having overlapping functionalities and search results' body content and old conversations accumulating unchanged. Anthropic considers hardcoding complex and fragile logic into the prompt as one kind of failure, and treating the proliferation of tools—leading to ambiguity about which tool to use—as a common failure. If even human engineers cannot determine which tool to use, then agents also struggle to perform effectively. In this state, even with a large number of tokens, the signal contributing to meaningful results is minimal, resulting in a low signal-to-noise ratio.

states.label: Curated context
states.body: Context engineering involves curating the entire set of tokens input into a model at the time of inference. Going beyond simply crafting a good prompt, it encompasses tool outputs, logs, and external data. The goal is to identify the smallest set of tokens with the highest signal-to-noise ratio that maximizes the likelihood of the desired outcome. The system prompt is carefully crafted at a high level to balance fragile, complex logic with ambiguous instructions, tools are designed to return sparse and token-efficient results, and instead of listing rules sequentially, a few diverse and representative examples are provided. Agents within loops repeatedly perform this curation, generating new data on each turn.

screens.outro: Then, when should the required information be inserted into the context? We will examine the strategy regarding the timing of retrieval.

screens.title: JIT Context and Hybrid Strategy
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare how the content contextualized within the same codebase questions differs by approach.

tabs.label: Pre-loading
tabs.body: This approach involves first retrieving relevant materials beforehand and inserting them into the context before performing inference using embedding-based search. Since it leverages already-computed data, it is fast. However, it may also include materials loosely related to the query, thereby consuming more attention budget.

tabs.label: JIT
tabs.body: JIT stands for "just in time." Instead of holding onto heavy context like full datasets, agents only carry lightweight identifiers such as file paths, stored queries, or web links. When needed, they fetch data into context using tools. Claude Code performs targeted queries on large datasets, viewing only parts of the data—such as heads or tails—without loading the entire dataset into context. Folder structures, file names, and timestamps also serve as useful signals.

tabs.label: The Price of JIT
tabs.body: Runtime exploration is slower than pre-computed search. Additionally, the agent must carefully design the tools and instructions to use during exploration to ensure it does not misuse tools, pursue dead ends, or miss critical information. Without proper guidance, JIT ends up wasting context.

tabs.label: Hybrid
tabs.body: Some data is pre-loaded for speed, while the rest is explored by the agent when needed. Claude Code pre-loads files such as CLAUDE.md into the context and immediately searches the remainder using tools like glob and grep. The degree to which autonomy is delegated depends on the task at hand; pre-loading may be more appropriate for stable content that changes infrequently.

screens.outro: Since we've verified the principle, let's apply it to a case where 50 search results have accumulated.

screens.title: Explanation: When the search results of 50 items were directly inserted.
screens.lead: The instructor demonstrates a step-by-step explanation of a situation where the search tool returns 50 results directly as full text, and shows improvement methods. Select the right arrow to follow along.

visual.alt: A bar chart comparing the context with full search results (50 items inserted directly into the body) versus the context containing only identifiers and summaries.
labels: Problem status: 50 entries in the body
Identifier and one-line summary for 50 items
Only three body items are needed.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: The agent received a request to "organize the history of refund policy changes for this quarter" and invoked a search tool. The tool returned 50 results verbatim, and the agent placed all of them in context. Only a few of these results were directly relevant to the request.

steps.title: Stage 1: Input token surge
steps.body: Fifty documents are loaded into the context at once, causing a sharp increase in input tokens. Since all prior content is re-inputted each turn, this document increases both cost and latency across all subsequent turns. A single tool call thus raises the cost of all subsequent work.

steps.title: Step 2: Signal-to-noise ratio decline
steps.body: When irrelevant text is mixed in, the proportion of content contributing to the context and resulting output decreases. The model spends a significant portion of its attention budget reading useless text. For the same number of tokens, most of the content becomes noise rather than meaningful signals.

steps.title: Step 3: Instructions and key outcomes are identified
steps.body: Recalling the initial instruction and the significant outcomes is blurred by the placement between the opening and the main body, revealing that the agent outputs in an incorrect format or re-identifies facts already verified. This is not a model issue but a result of context design.

steps.title: Improvement 1: Switch to JIT
steps.body: The tool only retains the result's identifier and a one-line summary in the context, while the agent retrieves the full body only when necessary. This is a typical application of just-in-time (JIT) retrieval, where lightweight identifiers such as file paths or links are held and fetched via the tool when needed. The context contains only a list and a summary, keeping it small and highly signal-rich.

steps.title: Improvement 2: Keep only relevant high-quality items
steps.body: Keep only the most relevant few entries and remove the rest from the context. Even after reading a passage once and drawing a conclusion, there's no need to retain it in the context. The tool may reduce what remains based on its design to return token-efficient results.

steps.title: One more thing: price discovery
steps.body: JIT is not free. Every time the main content is reloaded, an additional tool call may occur, leading to slower performance, and guidance is needed to determine which summary to report and what to open. Therefore, a hybrid approach—preloading frequently used, stable information and loading the rest via JIT—is a realistic choice.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: The key is not to make things small, but to make them precise. If an agent lacks necessary information, it will speculate; if it has excessive irrelevant information, the core focus becomes diluted. Context engineering is the process of identifying the smallest set of high-significance signals that maximizes the likelihood of a correct outcome.

screens.outro: I will conclude with one sentence capturing the essence.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Context should not be small; it should be accurate.
screens.lead: Summarizes the principles of context engineering.

paragraphs: Context is a finite resource, and as tokens increase, recall becomes blurred, leading to a diminished sense of harvest. Therefore, the goal of context engineering is to create the smallest set of high-significance token elements that maximizes the likelihood of achieving the desired outcome. Here, "small" does not mean "short." For an agent to act appropriately, it must have sufficient information, and that information must not be obscured by noise.

When determining how to retrieve required information, JIT is the default approach. Use lightweight identifiers to load information only when needed, but for performance-critical, stable data, employ a hybrid pre-loaded approach. The system prompt maintains an appropriate level of detail, tools are kept non-overlapping, and examples are limited to a few representative cases.

Start by identifying what occupies the most space in your agent's context. Typically, this consists of tool outputs, most of which are content that doesn't require reprocessing after being read once. Begin by checking whether you can identify and summarize such content using identifiers and summaries.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Context being large is not a boast but a burden. The criterion is not size, but the proportion of signals contributing to the outcome.

glossary.def: This is the scope of all text referenced when the model generates a response and also serves as working memory. The output is included.
It involves curating and maintaining all tokens input into the model at the inference stage.
This is a approach where lightweight identifiers are held, and data is fetched into context only when needed.
The ratio of information that contributes to the results versus information that does not.
The phenomenon where, as the token count increases, the model's ability to accurately recall information from context decreases.

misconceptions.myth: If the window is large, you can put everything in.
misconceptions.fact: Even with a larger window, accuracy and recall can degrade. Curating the content that is included remains increasingly important as the window grows.

misconceptions.myth: Context engineering is about writing good prompts.
misconceptions.fact: A prompt is only a part of it. It encompasses the entire input to the model, including tool results, conversation history, and external data.

misconceptions.myth: Information must be pre-filled entirely to be safe.
misconceptions.fact: JIT, which loads and retrieves components on demand via identifiers, consumes attention budget. However, hybrid preloading may be more effective for stable and frequently used information.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Context does not have to be smaller; it must be accurate.
The more tokens there are, the lower the recall becomes; therefore, the goal is to achieve the smallest high-signal subset.
The required information is loaded via JIT, and a hybrid approach is used that pre-inserts only some components when necessary.
First, verify whether the tool's output occupies a significant portion of the context.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What is causing noise in my context?

checks.q: When a search tool returns dozens of results as full texts, what would be most appropriate using a JIT context approach?
options: All content is pre-loaded, and the model selects it automatically.
Only brings the body text with just the identifier and one-line summary, loading only the necessary tools.
Keep the context window expanded to a larger model and maintain it entirely.
Lists all rules for every scenario in the system prompt.
checks.explain: JIT loads only light identifiers such as file paths or links, bringing them in only when necessary. Even if the window is large, it is not good to include many; the goal is the smallest set of high-signal tokens.

wrong.0: Irrelevant content lowers the signal-to-noise ratio and increases cost and delay.
wrong.2: Even with a large window, recall degrades as tokens accumulate, making curation essential.
wrong.3: Rules that list all possible cases are vulnerable and exemplary instances of a few specific cases are preferable.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded or graded.

checks.q: When placing the 50 search results directly into the context, arrange them in the order in which issues arise.
items: Input tokens surge, leading to higher costs and delays from the next turn.
Mixed content unrelated to the question reduces the signal-to-noise ratio.
Recollections become blurred between initial instructions and a large body of core results.
checks.explain: Token surges increase costs, turn irrelevant content into noise, and ultimately obscure critical instructions. The solution is to retain only high-relevance identifiers in a JIT (Just-In-Time) approach.
checks.intro: Let's try arranging the steps in order to clarify the flow. The results are not recorded or graded.
